items.prompt: Why can a turtle never leave its shell the way a hermit crab leaves its borrowed one?

options.label: The shell is glued to the skin by a thick layer of natural adhesive
options.feedback: No glue holds the shell on; the connection runs far deeper than the skin, straight into the turtle's own bones.

options.label: The shell is simply too heavy for the turtle to lift off
options.feedback: Weight is not the issue at all; even a turtle strong enough to lift its shell could not separate from it, because the two are not two separate objects to begin with.

options.label: The shell's bones are fused to the turtle's own spine and ribs
options.feedback: The domed upper shell is built from the turtle's own ribs and backbone, broadened and fused together, so shell and skeleton are literally the same structure.

options.label: The turtle grows a new shell each year and cannot shed the old one
options.feedback: A turtle's shell is not shed and regrown yearly; it is the same shell, part of the same skeleton, throughout its life.

items.ok_line: Shell and skeleton are one and the same structure.
items.ko_line: This is not about weight or glue; think about what the shell is actually made from.
items.exp_title: A shell that is also the skeleton
items.exp_text: A turtle's domed upper shell is built from its own ribs and backbone, flattened and broadened until they fuse into a single continuous plate rather than staying as separate curved bones under muscle. Because of this, the shell is not a container the turtle sits inside, the way a hermit crab occupies a borrowed shell it can abandon. It is the turtle's own skeleton, reshaped, which is why no turtle can ever climb out of its shell and leave it behind.

items.prompt: Why does a turtle flinch if you scratch the surface of its shell?

options.label: The shell is living bone covered in a thin layer richly supplied with nerves
options.feedback: Beneath the tough outer covering lies living bone and a network of nerve endings, so pressure or scratching on the shell is felt much the way touch is felt anywhere else on the body.

options.label: The shell has no feeling at all, and the flinch is only a reflex
options.feedback: The flinch is not a feeling-free reflex; it happens because the shell genuinely carries nerve endings capable of registering touch.

options.label: Scratching releases a chemical from the shell that irritates the skin nearby
options.feedback: No chemical release is involved; the sensation comes directly from nerves running through the shell itself, not from skin nearby reacting to something released.

options.label: The shell vibrates and shakes the turtle's inner organs when touched
options.feedback: A light scratch does not shake anything inside the body; the response comes from nerve endings in the shell detecting the touch directly, not from any internal vibration.

items.ok_line: Living bone with nerves running through it feels touch directly.
items.ko_line: This is not a numb reflex or a chemical release; the shell itself is genuinely able to feel.
items.exp_text: Unlike a fingernail or a suit of armor, a turtle's shell is made of living bone, covered by a thin layer of tough material and supplied throughout with blood vessels and nerve endings. Because those nerves run through the shell itself, pressure, scratching or injury there is genuinely felt, much as a touch anywhere else on the body would be. This is also why an injured shell can bleed and needs to heal, rather than simply flaking off the way a broken fingernail does.

items.prompt: How does a turtle breathe, given that its ribs are fused into its shell and cannot expand and contract the way ours do?

options.label: It absorbs oxygen directly through the shell's surface instead of using lungs
options.feedback: Some turtles can take in a small amount of oxygen through skin near the tail in water, but this is not how ordinary breathing works; the lungs still do the main job, and they still need to be filled and emptied.

options.label: Muscles around its limb openings and belly pump the lungs instead
options.feedback: With the ribcage locked in place as part of the shell, muscles attached near the limbs and along the belly take over the job of squeezing and releasing the lungs, moving air in and out in their place.

options.label: It holds its breath for extended periods and rarely needs to breathe
options.feedback: Turtles do breathe regularly on land; some species can hold their breath a long while underwater, but that is a separate matter from how the basic mechanics of breathing work at all.

options.label: Its neck muscles expand to draw air in like a bellows
options.feedback: The neck is used for reaching air at the surface or pulling the head in, not for powering the lungs; that job falls to muscles around the limbs and belly instead.

items.ok_line: Other muscles take over the pumping job the ribs can no longer do.
items.ko_line: The lungs are still filled and emptied by muscle, just not by an expanding ribcage; think about what other muscles could do that job.
items.exp_text: In most animals, muscles between the ribs expand and contract the chest to draw air in and push it out, but a turtle's ribs are fixed permanently in place as part of the shell and cannot move that way. Instead, muscles anchored around the openings where the limbs and neck emerge, along with muscles across the belly, contract to squeeze the lungs and relax to let them expand again. The whole breathing motion is powered from around the shell's edges rather than from a flexing ribcage inside it.

items.prompt: How does a tortoise pull its head safely inside its shell?

options.label: It briefly loosens the joints connecting its skull to its spine
options.feedback: No joints are loosened for this; the skull stays firmly connected to the spine the whole time, and it is the neck's own curve that does the retracting.

options.label: It folds its neck sideways against its own shoulder
options.feedback: Folding the neck sideways is how a different group of turtles retracts, not the S-shaped vertical folding many familiar tortoises use.

options.label: Strong shell muscles squeeze the opening shut around a fixed head position
options.feedback: The shell opening does not close around the head like a drawstring; the head itself is the part that moves, drawn backward by the neck.

options.label: Its neck bends into a tight S-curve, pulled back by strong muscles
options.feedback: The many small bones of the neck allow it to fold into a vertical S-shape, and muscles anchored along the spine draw this folded neck straight back into the shell.

items.ok_line: An S-shaped fold in the neck draws the head safely back.
items.ko_line: Nothing about the skull's joints or the shell's opening changes here; think about the shape the neck itself folds into.
items.exp_title: A neck that folds like a letter S
items.exp_text: A tortoise's neck is made of enough small bones, each with some flexibility, that it can bend into a tight vertical S-shape rather than staying straight. Strong muscles anchored along the spine draw this folded neck backward, pulling the head down and in behind the front edge of the shell until it is largely protected. Released again, the same muscles let the neck unfold back into its straight, extended position, ready to stretch the head back out.

items.prompt: How do sea turtle hatchlings find their way back, years later, to nest on the very beach where they hatched?

options.label: They sense the Earth's magnetic field and remember it like a set of coordinates
options.feedback: Hatchlings imprint on the particular magnetic signature of their home beach as they first enter the water, and years later a built-in sense of that same magnetic field guides them back to the same stretch of coast.

options.label: They follow the scent trail left by their mother in the sand
options.feedback: No scent trail from the mother survives years at sea; the guidance instead comes from a magnetic sense imprinted when the hatchling first left the beach.

options.label: They memorize the position of coastal landmarks as hatchlings
options.feedback: A hatchling only briefly sees the shoreline before swimming far out to sea, nowhere near long enough to memorize landmarks it could later use across an ocean crossing.

options.label: They are guided back by older turtles traveling the same route
options.feedback: Sea turtles do not travel in guided groups this way; each one navigates independently using a sense of its own, not by following others.

items.ok_line: A magnetic sense, imprinted early, guides the return years later.
items.ko_line: No scent, landmark, or guide is involved across an ocean crossing; think about a sense that would still work far out at sea.
items.exp_text: As a hatchling first crawls into the surf, it appears to imprint on the unique magnetic signature of that particular stretch of coastline, sensed through cells attuned to the Earth's magnetic field. Years later, after crossing vast distances of open ocean where no landmark or scent could possibly guide it, that same magnetic sense lets an adult female steer back toward the coordinates matching where she herself once hatched. Guided this way, she can return to nest remarkably close to her own birthplace among countless miles of coastline.

items.prompt: Why does the temperature of the sand around sea turtle eggs matter so much to the nest?

options.label: Cooler sand produces larger hatchlings, and warmer sand smaller ones
options.feedback: Size at hatching is not what incubation temperature primarily controls; the key effect it has is on something else about the developing hatchlings.

options.label: Warmer sand simply speeds up hatching without affecting the hatchlings themselves
options.feedback: Temperature does affect how quickly the eggs develop, but its more striking effect on the nest is not about timing alone.

options.label: It determines whether hatchlings develop as mostly male or mostly female
options.feedback: Unlike animals whose sex is fixed by chromosomes, a sea turtle's sex develops in response to the temperature the egg experiences, with warmer sand tending to produce more females and cooler sand more males.

options.label: It decides which hatchlings will be strong swimmers
options.feedback: Swimming ability is not what incubation temperature sets; its clearest, well-documented effect on the nest concerns something else entirely.

items.ok_line: Temperature during incubation shapes the mix of sexes in the nest.
items.ko_line: This is not about size, speed, or swimming; think about what temperature could set permanently during development.
items.exp_text: A sea turtle hatchling's sex is not fixed by chromosomes the way ours is; instead it develops in response to the temperature the egg experiences during a key stretch of incubation in the sand. Warmer sand tends to steer development toward female hatchlings, while cooler sand tends to steer it toward males, through the effect that temperature has on hormone activity inside the developing egg. A single nest can therefore skew heavily toward one sex or the other depending on nothing more than how warm its patch of sand happened to be.

items.prompt: How does a desert tortoise survive for months at a time without drinking any water?

options.label: It produces water internally by breaking down its own shell
options.feedback: The shell is not consumed for water; it stays intact and serves an entirely different purpose, that of protection.

options.label: It stores water in a large bladder and can slowly reabsorb it as needed
options.feedback: A desert tortoise can hold a substantial reserve of water in its bladder, drawing on that stored supply gradually over long dry stretches, alongside moisture taken in from the plants it eats.

options.label: It stops all internal water loss completely during dry periods
options.feedback: Some water loss continues no matter what; the tortoise instead manages this loss by drawing on a stored reserve, not by halting it entirely.

options.label: It absorbs water vapor directly from the desert air at night
options.feedback: Desert air holds very little moisture to begin with, and a tortoise does not draw water from it this way; its supply instead comes from what it has already stored and from its food.

items.ok_line: A large stored reserve, drawn on slowly, gets it through the dry stretch.
items.ko_line: Nothing about the shell or the night air is involved; think about a reserve the tortoise carries with it.
items.exp_text: A desert tortoise can hold a substantial volume of water in its bladder, built up whenever rain or a good meal makes water available, and it draws on this reserve gradually rather than all at once. Moisture taken in from the plants it eats adds further to this supply, stretching how long the stored water needs to last. By spending this reserve carefully and losing as little as possible along the way, a desert tortoise can go for months between the rare occasions when standing water is actually available.

items.prompt: Why does a tortoise's feet look round and stumpy, rather than webbed like an aquatic turtle's?

options.label: They act like sturdy pillars, bearing the shell's weight directly on land
options.feedback: Built more like columns than paddles, a tortoise's rounded feet distribute the heavy weight of its shell straight down into the ground with each step, which is what walking on land under that load requires.

options.label: They are simply an earlier stage a young tortoise later outgrows
options.feedback: A tortoise's feet do not change shape into something else as it matures; the sturdy, column-like shape it hatches with is the shape suited to its life on land throughout its whole life.

options.label: They help the tortoise dig extensive tunnels underground
options.feedback: Some tortoises do dig burrows, but the round, weight-bearing shape of the feet is explained by supporting the shell on land, not primarily by digging.

options.label: They reduce the tortoise's total body weight for easier movement
options.feedback: Foot shape has little effect on overall body weight; what it does affect is how that weight is supported and carried while walking.

items.ok_line: Sturdy, column-like feet carry the shell's weight on land.
items.ko_line: This is about supporting weight while walking, not about digging, growth stages, or overall weight.
items.exp_text: An aquatic turtle's webbed feet spread out into broad paddles that push against water efficiently, but that same shape would offer little support for a heavy shell pressing straight down onto solid ground. A tortoise's feet instead are rounded and compact, built more like the legs of a table than like paddles, so that each step bears the shell's considerable weight directly downward without buckling. This sturdier shape suits a life spent walking on land far better than it would suit a life spent swimming.

items.prompt: How can a domed tortoise flipped onto its back sometimes manage to right itself again?

options.label: It inflates air sacs inside its shell to tip itself upright
options.feedback: No internal air sacs exist for this purpose; the righting effort instead comes from the tortoise pushing physically against the ground with its neck and legs.

options.label: It waits motionless until another tortoise comes to help flip it over
options.feedback: A tortoise does not depend on help from others to right itself; the mechanism that lets it recover is built into its own shape and its own movements.

options.label: The flat underside of its shell rocks it back over on its own
options.feedback: A flat underside would not rock a tortoise back over by itself; what matters is the curved shape of the domed upper shell, combined with the tortoise's own pushing motion.

options.label: It uses its neck and legs to rock its highly domed shell until it tips back over
options.feedback: Stretching its neck out and pushing against the ground with its legs, a tortoise can rock its body side to side, and the curve of a sufficiently domed shell lets that rocking motion carry it past the tipping point and back onto its feet.

items.ok_line: Pushing and rocking against the curve of its own shell can tip it back over.
items.ko_line: No air sacs or outside help are involved; think about how the tortoise's own neck, legs, and shell shape work together.
items.exp_title: Rocking against the curve of its own shell
items.exp_text: A highly domed shell has a rounded shape that, once tipped even slightly off balance, wants to keep rolling rather than settle flat. A tortoise on its back can exploit this by stretching its neck out to one side and pushing hard against the ground with its legs, rocking its body further and further until the shell's own curve carries it past the tipping point. Not every tortoise manages this, since a flatter shell offers far less help, but a strongly domed one gives the rocking motion something to work with.

items.prompt: Why does a nesting sea turtle appear to cry thick tears while laying her eggs on a beach, far from any obvious cause for distress?

options.label: Sand irritates her eyes and triggers ordinary watering
options.feedback: Loose sand blowing about does not explain this; the fluid is produced continuously and in far greater volume than ordinary eye irritation would cause.

options.label: Glands near her eyes are expelling excess salt taken in from the sea
options.feedback: Living entirely in salty seawater and eating salty prey, a sea turtle takes in far more salt than her kidneys alone can remove, so specialized glands near the eyes work constantly to expel the excess, producing a thick, tear-like fluid.

options.label: The physical effort of digging the nest causes her to tear up
options.feedback: Physical exertion elsewhere in the body does not explain fluid produced specifically near the eyes; the real cause is a dedicated gland working there, unrelated to how tired her muscles are.

options.label: She is reacting to being out of water and struggling to breathe
options.feedback: Sea turtles breathe air normally and are not struggling for breath on land; the fluid near the eyes comes from a gland doing an entirely different job, unrelated to breathing.

items.ok_line: It is a salt gland at work, not sadness or discomfort.
items.ko_line: This has nothing to do with sand, effort, or breathing; think about what living in seawater does to her body's salt balance.
items.exp_title: A gland built to get rid of salt
items.exp_text: A sea turtle spends nearly her entire life in salty ocean water and feeds on salty prey, taking in far more salt than her kidneys are able to clear from her blood on their own. To cope with this, specialized glands positioned near each eye work continuously to filter excess salt out and expel it as a thick, concentrated fluid. On land the fluid runs visibly down her face since there is no seawater to wash it away at once, giving the appearance of tears where none of the usual causes for crying are present.
